title: The breath the demons couldn't pierce
hook: the gods and the demons were at war, and the gods reached for a song. the Chandogya tells which breath could carry it
carry: prana: the breath evil couldn't pierce
tomorrow: do the sounds between the words matter?

segments.voice: Yesterday: om is the essence of all essences. The Chandogya's chain ran from earth, water and food through voice and verse to the chant, and at its heart, Om.

The gods and the demons were at war. That's how the story starts, in the second section of the Chandogya Upanishad. And the gods decide their weapon will be a song. Not a spear, not a trick: the udgitha, the high chant. With this, they say, we'll overcome them. But a chant needs something to carry it, so the gods try one part of a person after another, and the demons follow them to each. Today: which breath can hold the song.
screen: `THE GODS AND THE DEMONS AT WAR.` → `THE GODS REACH FOR A SONG.` → `WHAT CAN CARRY IT?`

segments.voice: In paraphrase, it goes like this. First the gods sing the chant as the breath in the nose. The demons pierce it with evil, and that, the text says, is why we smell both the sweet and the foul. Next, speech. Pierced: that's why we speak both truth and falsehood. Then the eye, and we see both what's fitting and what isn't. Then the ear, and we hear both. Then the mind, and we think both kinds of thoughts. Each one cracks. Then the gods sing the chant as the breath in the mouth, the main breath, the one that keeps a body alive. The demons rush at it and scatter, the text says, the way a lump of earth flung at a solid rock breaks into pieces. Here's the teaching folded inside. Every sense in us is mixed; the same tongue blesses and lies. But underneath them is prana, the life-breath, going in and out on good days and bad, and in this story it's the one thing evil couldn't break. So the high chant is sung as prana: the song rides on the breath that keeps the singer alive. Hindu practice still puts the breath first. In sandhya, the daily prayers at dawn and dusk built around the Gayatri, a few rounds of pranayama, measured breathing, come before the mantra, and many formal pujas open the same way. Many teachers read this story as one old reason why: before you pray with a voice that can go either way, you begin from the breath that can't.
screen: `NOSE, SPEECH, EYE, EAR, MIND: PIERCED.` · `EACH ONE GOES BOTH WAYS.` · `THE MAIN BREATH: THE DEMONS SCATTER.` · `IN SANDHYA, THE BREATH COMES FIRST.` · then, large: `PRANA: THE BREATH EVIL COULDN'T PIERCE.`

segments.voice: Notice a smell in the room, a sound, a thought passing, each with its own mood. Then let them go and come to the breath: in slowly through the nose, a short easy pause, out slowly, the measured breath many Hindus take before sandhya or puja. Keep it gentle and never strain; if anything feels uncomfortable, just breathe normally. A few rounds, then rest in the plain breath. If you pray, let that breath carry your prayer.
The Sama Veda as song. In the Chandogya, the high chant can't be carried by the senses or the mind. It's sung as the main breath, prana. Today's word.
screen: `THE SAMA VEDA AS SONG — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: prana, the breath evil couldn't pierce. The song rides on it. See you tomorrow.

original.note: Sanskrit: breath, life-breath. In Chandogya 1.2 the high chant is sung as the main breath.

chat.meaning: In Chandogya 1.2 the demons pierce smell, speech, sight, hearing and mind, so each goes both ways; the main breath, prana, holds, and the chant is sung as it. Sandhya also puts pranayama before the Gayatri.

Chandogya Upanishad.meaning: an Upanishad of the Sama Veda tradition

udgitha.meaning: the high chant the lead singer sends up

pranayama.meaning: measured breathing, done before sandhya and many pujas

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 1.2.1–8 (the gods and demons; the udgitha as nose-breath, speech, eye, ear, mind, then the main breath)
Sandhyavandana: pranayama before the Gayatri japa; pranayama at the opening of formal puja

notes: Paraphrase of Chandogya 1.2.1–8: confirm the order of the five pierced faculties (nose-breath, speech, eye, ear, mind) and the image of the clod of earth striking a rock.
'Both sides are children of the same creator' renders the text's devāsurā ... prājāpatyāḥ; confirm.
'The breath in the mouth, the main breath' renders mukhya prāṇa / āsanya prāṇa; confirm wording.
'Almost funny in its plainness' is tone, not a claim about the text; cut if a Keeper finds it light.
The line 'demons' is used for asuras; some teachers prefer 'asuras' or 'anti-gods'.
